question: Why do you want to study actuarial science specifically, rather than maths or economics on its own?
lookingFor: A genuine reason for wanting the applied, professional blend of maths, statistics, and business rather than a pure discipline.

bullets: Name what actuarial science actually is: using probability and statistics to measure and price financial risk
Explain why the applied, professional angle appeals more than pure theory
Ground it in a concrete moment that sparked the interest
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've always liked maths best when it's solving a real problem rather than sitting in the abstract, and actuarial science is exactly that, using probability to answer questions like how much a pension fund needs to set aside today. I looked into pure maths degrees but I want the statistics to be pointed at something with real financial consequences. A school project where we modelled how long a class set of laptops would last before needing replacement got me hooked on that kind of forward-looking calculation, and I want to build a career doing it properly.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I'm good at maths' with no sense of what actuaries actually do
Confusing actuarial science with accounting or general finance
Giving a reason that would apply equally to any quantitative degree
followUps: What do you understand an actuary's day-to-day work to actually involve?

question: Why do you want to study actuarial science at this university in particular?
lookingFor: Specific, researched reasons tied to this course's structure, exemptions, or staff, not generic praise.

bullets: Reference something concrete about the course, such as professional body exam exemptions
Connect it to how you personally learn or what you want from your degree
Show you've compared it against alternatives, not just applied by default
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Your course carries exemptions from several of the professional actuarial exams, which matters a lot to me because I know qualifying fully takes years of exams even after graduating, so starting that clock early is a real advantage. I also liked that the second year includes a placement year option, because I want to test the day-to-day reality of the job before committing my twenties to the exams. I looked at two other courses and this one had the clearest path from degree into a graduate actuarial scheme, which is exactly what I'm after.

commonMistakes: Citing rankings or reputation with no course specifics
Not knowing about professional body exemptions at all
A generic answer that could apply to any university offering the subject
followUps: What would you do if you didn't get all the exemptions you're hoping for?

question: What first got you interested in becoming an actuary?
lookingFor: A believable, specific moment or process, not a rehearsed line about liking maths and money.

bullets: Tell a specific, small story rather than a vague claim
Show the interest developed rather than appeared instantly
Link it to what actuaries actually do, not just 'I like numbers'
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My uncle works in pensions and one Christmas he explained why our family's life insurance premiums went up after a health scare, walking me through roughly how the insurer was pricing the extra risk. I found it fascinating that you could put a number on something as uncertain as someone's future health. That sent me down a bit of a rabbit hole reading about mortality tables, and by the time I was choosing A-levels I'd already picked further maths and economics with this in mind.

commonMistakes: A generic 'I've always loved maths' with no specific trigger
Describing an interest in finance broadly rather than risk and probability specifically
Sounding rehearsed rather than like an actual memory
followUps: Has your understanding of the job changed since then?

question: How would you explain to a twelve year old what an actuary actually does?
lookingFor: The ability to simplify a technical role without dumbing it down to nonsense, showing real understanding underneath.

bullets: Use a simple, relatable analogy rather than jargon
Capture the core idea of pricing uncertain future events
Keep it accurate even while simplifying
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd say an actuary is like someone who gets paid to guess the future carefully, using maths instead of a crystal ball. If an insurance company wants to know how much to charge for car insurance, an actuary looks at data on thousands of past drivers and works out how likely a crash is and how much it would cost, then turns that into a fair price. It's less about predicting one person's future and more about being very accurate on average across huge groups of people.

commonMistakes: Using technical terms a twelve year old wouldn't understand
Oversimplifying to the point of being inaccurate, like 'they just guess numbers'
Confusing the actuary's role with a general banker or accountant
followUps: What's the difference between what an actuary does and what an accountant does?

question: What's the difference between an actuary and an accountant?
lookingFor: A clear grasp that actuaries look forward under uncertainty while accountants record and report what has already happened.

bullets: State that accountants deal mainly with recording and reporting past financial transactions
State that actuaries model future uncertain events and their financial cost
Give an example that makes the distinction concrete
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: An accountant is mostly looking backward, they record what a company earned and spent and make sure the books are accurate and compliant. An actuary is looking forward into genuine uncertainty, working out things like how much an insurer should charge today for a risk that might or might not happen in thirty years. So if a company wants to know last quarter's profit, that's an accountant's question, but if they want to know how much to set aside for pension payouts to staff who haven't even retired yet, that's an actuarial one.

commonMistakes: Treating the two roles as interchangeable
Only describing one profession and assuming the other is similar
No concrete example to anchor the distinction
followUps: Where might an actuary and an accountant work together on the same problem?

question: Why does insurance work? What's the underlying idea that lets an insurer charge people to cover unpredictable events?
lookingFor: Understanding of risk pooling and the law of large numbers, not just 'they collect premiums and pay claims'.

bullets: Explain that pooling many independent risks makes the group outcome predictable even when individuals aren't
Mention the law of large numbers or something equivalent in plain language
Note that the premium has to cover expected claims plus a margin for expenses and profit
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: No single person can predict whether their house will burn down, but across a hundred thousand houses, an insurer can predict fairly accurately how many fires will happen in a year, because individual randomness smooths out over a large enough group. That's the law of large numbers in action. So the insurer collects a premium from everyone that reflects the average expected cost per person, plus a bit extra for expenses and profit, and uses that pool to pay the unlucky few whose houses actually burn down. It only works because the risks are largely independent of each other.

commonMistakes: Describing insurance as just collecting money and hoping claims are low
Not mentioning why pooling many people makes outcomes predictable
Ignoring that risks need to be reasonably independent for pooling to work well
followUps: What happens to this logic when risks aren't independent, like in a flood or a pandemic?

question: You mentioned risk pooling works best when risks are independent. What goes wrong for an insurer when risks are correlated, like flood damage across a whole town?
lookingFor: Understanding that correlated risk breaks the diversification benefit and can threaten insurer solvency, plus awareness of how insurers respond.

bullets: Explain that correlated risks can all trigger at once, wiping out the averaging benefit
Note the solvency risk this creates for the insurer
Mention real tools insurers use to manage it, like reinsurance or geographic diversification
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: If risks are correlated, the whole point of pooling breaks down, because instead of a few unlucky claims scattered through the year, you can get thousands of claims landing on the insurer at exactly the same time, like every house in a flooded town claiming together. That can threaten the insurer's ability to pay out at all, not just eat into profit. That's why insurers use reinsurance, essentially buying their own insurance against a catastrophic cluster of claims, and why they try to diversify their book across different regions and types of risk rather than concentrating in one flood-prone area. It's also why some catastrophic risks, like certain flood zones, become very expensive or hard to insure at all.

commonMistakes: Not connecting correlation to the breakdown of the law of large numbers
Ignoring reinsurance or diversification as real-world responses
Treating this as a purely theoretical problem with no solvency consequence
followUps: Can you think of another example of correlated risk actuaries have to worry about today?

question: Can you explain what expected value means, using a simple example?
lookingFor: A correct, clearly explained definition with a worked example, showing comfort with the core building block of actuarial maths.

bullets: State that expected value is the probability-weighted average of all possible outcomes
Walk through a simple worked example with numbers
Note that it's a long-run average, not a guaranteed single outcome
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Expected value is what you'd get on average if you repeated an uncertain event many, many times, calculated by multiplying each possible outcome by its probability and adding them up. So if a game pays you ten pounds with a fifty percent chance and nothing otherwise, the expected value is half of ten, which is five pounds. That doesn't mean any single play gives you five pounds, it's what your average payout would settle towards if you played the game thousands of times, and it's exactly the kind of calculation actuaries use to price something like an insurance premium.

commonMistakes: Confusing expected value with the most likely single outcome
Getting the calculation itself wrong
Giving a definition with no worked example
followUps: If the game cost six pounds to play, would you play it, and why?

question: Why is a pound today worth more than a pound in ten years? How does that idea matter to an actuary?
lookingFor: Understanding of the time value of money and discounting, connected to why it matters for pricing long-term liabilities.

bullets: Explain that money today can be invested and earn interest, so it grows
Mention inflation as a second reason future money buys less
Connect it to discounting future liabilities to work out what to set aside today
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A pound today can be invested and earn interest, so by the time ten years pass it could have grown into more than a pound, which means a pound promised in ten years is worth less today. Inflation adds to that, because prices tend to rise, so future money buys less than it would now. This matters hugely for actuaries because a lot of the work is about promises to pay money far in the future, like a pension in forty years, and you need to discount that future payment back to today's value to work out how much needs to be invested now to cover it.

commonMistakes: Only mentioning inflation and forgetting the investment growth angle, or vice versa
Not connecting the concept back to actuarial pricing or reserving
Confusing discounting with simply subtracting a fixed amount
followUps: How would a higher assumed interest rate change how much a pension fund needs today?

question: Becoming a fully qualified actuary usually takes several years of professional exams even after your degree. Are you prepared for that, and why do you think you'd stick with it?
lookingFor: Realistic awareness of the qualification path and evidence of persistence, not naive enthusiasm.

bullets: Show accurate awareness of the length and difficulty of professional qualification
Give real evidence of persistence from your own life, not just a promise
Show you've thought about studying alongside full-time work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I know it can take anywhere from three to six years of exams alongside a full-time job to become fully qualified, and that some exams have fairly low pass rates, so I've tried to be realistic rather than starry-eyed about it. What gives me confidence is that I've kept up grade seven piano alongside my A-levels for four years, which meant regular structured practice around a demanding timetable, and I know that discipline transfers. I'd rather go in with my eyes open about the exams than be surprised by them halfway through a graduate scheme.

commonMistakes: Not knowing that significant post-degree exams exist at all
Claiming persistence with no real evidence to back it up
Sounding intimidated rather than realistically prepared
followUps: What would you do if you failed one of those professional exams?

question: Have you read anything or followed any news that's shaped how you think about risk or the insurance industry?
lookingFor: Genuine engagement beyond the syllabus, with the ability to discuss the content, not just name-drop a title.

bullets: Name something specific, a book, article, or news story
Explain the actual content and what you took from it
Connect it to your own thinking about risk or the profession
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read 'The Signal and the Noise' by Nate Silver, and the chapter on why forecasters are often overconfident stuck with me, because it applies directly to actuarial work where being too certain about an assumption can be really costly. I've also been following news coverage of insurers pulling out of flood-prone and wildfire-prone areas in parts of the US, because it's a live example of a risk becoming genuinely uninsurable at a normal price. It made me realise actuarial work isn't just calculation, it also involves difficult judgement calls about what risks a market can even bear.

commonMistakes: Naming a book or article with no evidence of having actually engaged with it
Picking something totally unrelated to risk, insurance, or probability
Reciting a summary with no personal reflection
followUps: Did that reading change any opinion you held before?

question: What have you done to find out whether actuarial work is actually right for you?
lookingFor: Concrete, self-driven exposure to the field, such as insight days, spreadsheet projects, or conversations with actuaries.

bullets: Describe a specific activity, not just 'I researched it online'
Explain what you learned about the reality of the job, good or bad
Show initiative in seeking the experience out
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I did a virtual insight day with a general insurer where we worked through a simplified pricing exercise in a spreadsheet, adjusting a premium based on a claimant's age and location, and I found the mix of judgement and hard numbers really satisfying. I also emailed a local actuary I found through LinkedIn and she was kind enough to do a twenty minute call, where she was honest that the exam workload in your twenties is genuinely tough. That honesty actually made me more sure about it, because I'd rather know that going in than be surprised.

commonMistakes: Only citing generic online research with no active experience
Describing an experience that was entirely passive, like watching one video
Failing to reflect on what the experience actually revealed
followUps: What surprised you most from that experience?

question: Actuarial work increasingly involves coding and large datasets, not just formulas on paper. What experience do you have with that, and how do you feel about it?
lookingFor: Awareness that modern actuarial work is data-heavy, with some honest evidence of relevant skill or willingness to build it.

bullets: Show awareness that spreadsheets and code like Excel, R, or Python are core actuarial tools now
Give a specific example of your own experience, even if modest
Be honest about your current level while showing willingness to grow
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I know actuaries spend a lot of time in Excel and increasingly in R or Python, working with datasets far too big to handle by hand. I taught myself basic Python over the summer through a free online course and used it to build a simple simulation of a dice game to check my probability calculations against, which was a small project but it made the coding side feel less abstract. I wouldn't call myself advanced yet, but I genuinely enjoyed it and I'm keen to build on it properly during the degree.

commonMistakes: Assuming actuarial work is still all pen-and-paper formulas
Overstating coding ability that falls apart under a follow-up question
Showing no interest in or awareness of the data side of the role at all
followUps: What was the hardest part of that project for you?

question: Actuaries work across different areas like life insurance, general insurance, and pensions. Do you know the difference, and is any one of them of particular interest to you?
lookingFor: Basic awareness of the main practice areas, with an honest, thought-through preference or openness rather than a memorised list.

bullets: Distinguish life insurance and pensions, which deal with long time horizons and mortality, from general insurance, which deals with shorter-tail risks like cars or property
Show you've thought about which area interests you and why, or explain you're keeping an open mind
Avoid pretending certainty you don't actually have
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Life and pensions work deals with very long time horizons, thinking about mortality and how long people will live to work out pension payouts or life cover decades ahead. General insurance is usually shorter term, pricing things like car or home insurance where claims tend to settle within a year or two. I'm more drawn to general insurance at the moment, because I like that the data updates faster and you can see the impact of your pricing decisions sooner, but I know I've only had a small taste of either, so I want to stay open until I've actually tried both during a placement.

commonMistakes: Not knowing the practice areas exist at all
Claiming a passionate, fixed preference with nothing to back it up
Confusing general insurance with health insurance specifically
followUps: What would make you switch your preference after actually working in the field?

question: Imagine you're working on a pricing model and your manager asks you to use a more optimistic assumption to win a big client, even though you think it understates the real risk. What would you do?
lookingFor: Structured ethical reasoning that balances professional integrity, actuarial standards, and workplace realities, not a naive absolute stance.

bullets: Recognise the tension between commercial pressure and professional duty
Reason through steps, like raising the concern directly and asking for the evidence behind the assumption
Land on prioritising honesty and professional standards over pleasing a manager
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd want to understand first whether my manager has information I don't, because maybe there's a genuine reason the assumption is defensible that I'm missing, so I wouldn't just refuse outright. But if after that conversation I still believed the assumption was unjustifiably optimistic, I'd say so clearly and put my reasoning in writing, because actuaries have a professional duty to be honest about the risk they're modelling, even under commercial pressure. I understand actuaries can actually be personally accountable to their professional body for this kind of thing, so I wouldn't just go along with it to keep the peace, I'd escalate if I genuinely thought it was wrong.

commonMistakes: Immediately caving to the manager's request without any pushback
Refusing dramatically with no attempt to understand the manager's reasoning first
Not mentioning any professional or ethical duty at all
followUps: What if your manager was your direct boss and pushing back could hurt your career?

question: What is a mortality table and roughly how is it used?
lookingFor: Understanding of what mortality tables represent and how they're used to price life insurance or value pensions, without requiring exam-level detail.

bullets: Describe it as data showing the probability of death at each age, built from large historical populations
Explain it's used to work out expected payout timing and cost for life insurance or pensions
Note it can be adjusted for factors like smoking status or health
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A mortality table shows, for each age, the probability that a person of that age dies within the next year, usually built from large amounts of historical population data. Insurers use it to estimate how long a policyholder is likely to live, which lets them work out roughly when a life insurance payout or pension is likely to be needed and therefore how much to charge or set aside now. It's not a prediction about any one individual, it's a statistical tool, and insurers often adjust the base table for things like smoking status or existing health conditions to price more accurately for a specific person.

commonMistakes: Describing it as predicting an individual's exact lifespan
Not connecting it to pricing or reserving at all
Forgetting that tables get adjusted for individual risk factors
followUps: Why might mortality tables need updating over time?

question: What is a normal distribution, and why does it come up so often in statistics?
lookingFor: Correct description of the bell curve shape and mean/standard deviation, with some sense of why it appears so widely, such as the central limit theorem.

bullets: Describe the symmetric bell-shaped curve centred on the mean
Mention standard deviation as the measure of spread
Give some sense of why it's so common, such as via the central limit theorem
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A normal distribution is a symmetric, bell-shaped curve where most values cluster around the mean and become less likely the further you get from it, with the standard deviation describing how spread out the values are. It shows up constantly in statistics partly because of something called the central limit theorem, which says that if you add up lots of independent random effects, the total tends to look roughly normal even if the individual pieces don't. That's part of why it's such a useful default assumption in a lot of statistical and actuarial modelling, though I know it isn't always the right fit, especially for things like extreme insurance losses.

commonMistakes: Describing the shape without mentioning mean or standard deviation
Claiming everything in nature or finance is normally distributed
No mention of why it's so common statistically
followUps: Can you think of a situation in insurance where the normal distribution wouldn't be a good fit?

question: If you roll two fair six-sided dice, what's the probability that the sum is at least 10? Talk me through your reasoning.
lookingFor: Clear, methodical probabilistic reasoning worked out aloud, not just a memorised or guessed answer.

bullets: Set up the total number of equally likely outcomes correctly, which is 36
Systematically count the favourable outcomes for sums of 10, 11, and 12
State the final probability clearly and check it's sensible
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: There are 36 equally likely outcomes in total, since each die has six faces and they're independent. I need the sum to be 10, 11, or 12. For a sum of 10 there's four and six, five and five, and six and four, so three combinations. For 11 there's five and six and six and five, so two. For 12 there's only six and six, so one. That's three plus two plus one, which is six favourable outcomes out of 36, so the probability is six over 36, which simplifies to one sixth.

commonMistakes: Using the wrong total number of outcomes, like 11 instead of 36
Missing some combinations, such as forgetting both orderings
Jumping to an answer without showing any working
followUps: How would your approach change if the dice weren't fair?

question: What's a current issue facing the insurance or pensions industry that you find interesting, and why?
lookingFor: Genuine awareness of a real, current industry issue with some understanding of why it matters, not a vague headline recall.

bullets: Name a specific, current issue, such as climate risk, longevity risk, or AI in underwriting
Explain in your own words why it's a problem for actuaries specifically
Show some sense of the trade-offs or open questions involved
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I find the longevity risk problem interesting, the fact that people are living longer than pension funds originally assumed decades ago, which means some pension schemes have had to find more money than they planned for. It's a good example of how an actuarial assumption made years ago can turn out to be wrong in a way that has huge financial consequences, and it isn't obviously anyone's fault, it's just genuine uncertainty about the future. I think it's pushed the industry towards updating mortality assumptions more frequently and towards products like longevity swaps, which I'd like to understand better.

commonMistakes: Naming an issue with no real explanation of why it matters
Picking something that isn't actually actuarial or insurance related
Reciting a headline with no personal understanding behind it
followUps: How do you think the industry should respond to that issue?

question: What maths topics have you studied so far that you think will help you most in this degree, and which do you find hardest?
lookingFor: Honest, specific self-assessment of mathematical preparation relevant to actuarial content, like probability, statistics, or calculus.

bullets: Name specific topics studied, ideally probability, statistics, or calculus
Explain honestly which area is hardest and why
Show a plan or attitude for addressing the weaker area
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Statistics and probability have been my strongest areas, I really enjoyed the hypothesis testing module in my further maths course and did well in it. Calculus is where I have to work harder, especially integration by parts, it doesn't come as naturally to me as the probability side does. I've been going through extra practice problems over the summer because I know actuarial work leans on both, and I'd rather shore up that weaker area now than struggle with it once the pace of a degree picks up.

commonMistakes: Claiming to be equally strong at everything with no real weakness named
Naming topics with no honest reflection on strengths or gaps
Vague answer with no specific mathematical topic mentioned at all
followUps: What have you actually done to work on that weaker area?

question: Actuarial work can involve long stretches of detailed, technical, and sometimes repetitive analysis. What makes you think you'd actually enjoy that day to day?
lookingFor: Realistic self-knowledge about enjoying detailed, sustained technical work, backed by genuine past evidence.

bullets: Acknowledge the reality that the work can be detailed and unglamorous at times
Give real evidence from your own experience of enjoying similarly detailed work
Avoid overselling excitement that doesn't match the reality of the role
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I know a lot of the actual work is quite detailed, checking assumptions, tidying data, running the same model with slightly different inputs, and it isn't glamorous in the way it might sound from the outside. What tells me I'd genuinely enjoy it is that I've spent hours refining a spreadsheet model for our school's fundraising event, adjusting small assumptions and rechecking totals, and I found that kind of careful, iterative work satisfying rather than tedious. I like the feeling of a model getting more accurate the more care you put in, and I think that's the same instinct actuarial work rewards.

commonMistakes: Pretending the job is constantly exciting with no acknowledgment of the detailed reality
Giving no concrete evidence of enjoying similar detailed work before
Sounding uncertain about whether they'd actually enjoy it
followUps: Tell me about a time detailed work like that actually frustrated you.

question: Every actuarial model relies on assumptions about the future that could turn out to be wrong. How should an actuary handle that uncertainty responsibly?
lookingFor: Awareness that models are simplifications with real limitations, and a sense of practical ways to manage that uncertainty responsibly.

bullets: Acknowledge that all models are simplifications and assumptions can be wrong
Mention practical tools like sensitivity testing, margins for prudence, or scenario analysis
Note the importance of communicating uncertainty honestly rather than presenting a single number as certain
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think the first step is just being honest that a model is a simplification of reality, not reality itself, and treating every output as conditional on the assumptions behind it. Practically, that means testing how sensitive the results are if key assumptions shift, running a few different scenarios rather than relying on one central case, and often building in some margin for prudence so the model isn't overconfident. Just as important is communicating that uncertainty clearly to whoever is using the results, rather than handing over a single precise-looking number that hides how shaky some of the underlying assumptions really are.

commonMistakes: Treating model output as a guaranteed, certain fact
Naming no practical technique for managing uncertainty
Ignoring the communication side of the problem entirely
followUps: Can you think of a real historical example where a model's assumptions turned out badly wrong?

question: What would you bring to this course and to a cohort of other actuarial science students?
lookingFor: Self-aware, specific answer about a genuine strength or perspective, not a generic list of buzzwords.

bullets: Name a specific, genuine strength rather than a generic trait
Back it with a concrete example
Connect it to how it would actually help peers or group work in the course
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think I'd bring a habit of explaining things clearly, which comes from two years of tutoring younger students in maths, where I learned that if you can't explain a method simply, you probably don't understand it as well as you think. In a subject as technical as this, I think that's genuinely useful in group projects, being the person who checks that everyone actually follows the reasoning rather than just nodding along. I'd want to bring that same habit into study groups here, especially once the material gets harder for everyone.

commonMistakes: Listing generic traits like 'hardworking' with no evidence
Talking only about personal ambition with nothing about the cohort
Overselling with no concrete example to support the claim
followUps: Tell me about a specific time that strength actually helped a group you were part of.

question: Suppose a pricing model you built turns out, six months later, to have significantly underpriced a product because of a wrong assumption. What would you do?
lookingFor: A structured, responsible response covering acknowledging the error, understanding its cause, and correcting it, rather than panic or denial.

bullets: Prioritise flagging the error quickly and transparently rather than hiding it
Describe investigating why the assumption was wrong before making changes
Mention correcting the model and communicating the impact to stakeholders
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first instinct would be to flag it as soon as I was confident it was a genuine error, rather than sitting on it hoping it resolves itself, because the longer an underpriced product runs, the bigger the financial hole gets. Then I'd want to understand exactly why the assumption was wrong, whether it was a data issue, a change in the real world, or a mistake in my own reasoning, because the fix depends on the cause. After that I'd correct the model, document what changed and why, and make sure whoever relies on that pricing understands the impact going forward, since being upfront about a mistake early is far better than someone else discovering it later.

commonMistakes: Suggesting they'd quietly try to fix it without telling anyone
Jumping straight to a fix without investigating the actual cause
Showing panic rather than a structured response
followUps: How would you explain that mistake to a manager without sounding like you're making excuses?

question: Where do you see yourself within the actuarial profession in ten years, and how does this course set you up for that?
lookingFor: An ambitious but grounded direction linked clearly to what the course offers, showing realistic understanding of the qualification path.

bullets: Give a plausible direction within the profession, not an over-specific job title
Connect it honestly to what the course and its exemptions offer
Show openness to the direction shifting as they learn more
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: In ten years I'd like to be a fully qualified actuary working in general insurance, ideally on the pricing side where I can see the direct link between the models I build and real business decisions. This course matters to that plan because of the professional exam exemptions, which means I'm not starting the qualification process from zero the day I graduate, and the placement year would let me test that pricing interest against the reality of the job before I commit fully. I'm open to that changing, maybe I end up preferring pensions or a more research-focused role, but the exam-exempt path and the placement are what make this course the right foundation either way.

commonMistakes: An unrealistically precise ten-year plan with no room for change
A goal disconnected from anything the actual course offers
No awareness of the professional qualification timeline at all
followUps: What's the first concrete step you'd take in your first year to move toward that goal?
